chunks.text: Yeah. Oh. We're going to find a question that's for you now. We'll pass you some suggestions, Todd. Okay. Morning, Grant. It's great to have you back, and Andrew. And if you want to give a bit of a preamble and- Sure. Sure... and then we'll just have a pretty relaxed Q&A.

So I thought I could kick off with just a thumbnail reflection on the year to June. I've made some commitments to the House, and you've given me the opportunity to reflect back on progress, and so that'll be very short. And then spend a bit of time talking about, from our office's perspective, how we see the context within which the public service is operating and some of the change and therefore some of the inherent risks that come with that.

So yeah, off the back of that, a conversation about how we can enable scrutiny by Parliament in that environment, I think would be really helpful for us to go back and reflect on that in building up our future work program. So quickly, on the performance for the year ended June '26.

We still have an annoying tail of basic statutory audit arrears, but we're making progress. And it is still those very small entities in some schools, some of which have been wound up, and so it's a thing which I want to draw an end to, is chasing former boards of trustees to figure out who might be able to actually sign on behalf of the entity so that I can sign an audit report. So we're getting more granular in terms of understanding what's in that tail, which gives me confidence we're making progress.

If we look at the discretionary work program, we did eight pieces of performance audit work in the 12 months, and three follow-ups. There's probably four themes coming out of that discretionary work, which I'll just whip through now. But there's opportunities across those eight for agencies to better use the data they have in front of them to target their services.

And we can get into that later if the committee are interested. We have lots of meetings across ecosystems or sectors, but those meetings, in our view, are not being informed with joined-up information that enables concentrated discussion on the things those entities can do better together.

And so the inquiry work that this committee led, which we're awaiting on government response for, the notion of having a kind of framing of sectoral reporting, we think is going to be really important to elevating some of that focus in those cross-agency meetings onto topics that matter.

Strategic financial management capability, I think we've spoken to the committee previously about that. We've joined up with Treasury and PSC. It's an area of focus for the three of us. And there are some good things PSC in particular are leading in that space. But given everything else that's going on, we need the capability quickly in order to make some safe decisions around trade-offs going forward.

And sharing of data by agencies and better management, better measurement of and evaluation of the effectiveness of programs. SIA is doing some really good thinking and some really good work, but it's tiny in the scheme of social sector spend. So while we're encouraged by some of the things we're seeing in SIA, we're turning our minds to, well, how do we work with them in a way that provokes uptake of that thinking more quickly by more agencies?

In terms of the context, it's trite to say change is kind of a feature. We've got machinery of government ambitions which are at a different scale than we've seen for a very long time in this country or in fact, ever. We've got layers of reform impacting local government.

There's a real ambition to leverage the investment in data and AI technologies. There's a move to larger entities, a move to centralize things inside the central agencies like the GDDA. We don't have views whether these are the right or wrong things.

We just think change creates a unique set of inherent risks that we want to make sure that we're across and we're advising Parliament in the best way possible to enable you to be across them. So at one level, it's just change. But if I pick on, not pick on local government, but some of the water reform, the leg has happened, but now we've got entities trying to deal with the individual contexts they're operating in.

We've got the same people involved in amalgamation. And so it's the layering that is quite different to what we've seen in a part of our public service system, which has never had the best capabilities that the system has available to it. So the stretch on that sector in particular is something that we're acutely mindful of. And with the long-term planning around about to kick off, we're trying to be careful to make sure our assurance involvement is not distracting or slowing things down. But equally, the legislation requires us to audit, and audit's done to a standard.

So we're trying to be early and do all those good things, but the absorptive capacity in that sector in particular is something that really does get me kind of thinking, are we doing enough to support them? Sorry, but it's just the other things on my daily sheet of what's really driving my attention at the moment.

Large scale change, one thing we know from looking backwards is, there's inherent risks that you see a performance dip as you distract the workforce from delivering the services that New Zealanders need them to keep delivering. At the same time, we've said to the committee previously, we don't believe the performance frameworks that are across the public service sufficiently enable a real lens into what's actually going on under the hood.

So are they transparent enough so you know whether or not that uncertainty is actually creating a degradation of service delivery or not? So that's one thing we are spending some time on, and we'll try and integrate into our briefings to various committees, to make sure if we're seeing degradation of service, we're bringing that to the attention of the House.

Absorptive capacity is something that we're really mindful of. Centralization is a thing. We've all of an age where we've seen this, and I'm not saying it's a right or wrong model, but actually it comes with a whole bunch of inherent challenges, particularly around the risk of losing a local voice.

And so the way in which the center remains connected to the coalface where services are delivered becomes increasingly important because your ability to rely on those regional local relationships as a good source of intelligence, you need to think differently about how the center's getting access to those more real time pieces of information that allow you to understand where you might need to course-correct.

I'm telling you things you already know, but I guess what I'm trying to signal is, these are the things that I want my teams to be very mindful of in preparing the briefings for all committees, so that if everything's going fine and these inherent risk characteristics are being taken account of, I'll be the happiest man alive.

But we just need to make sure that we've got our eyes on them. Grant, do you mind if I kick off with a question? Go ahead. Mm-hmm. Firstly, I really like the plan. I thought it was really coherent and easy to follow along, given the complexity of government. So kudos to you and the team. I did wonder, through the... And I know you gave examples like on education, like school learner, the budgets for education, reaching school learner objectives and that sort of stuff.

Is that a bit of a hint of the work we did on the performance reporting stuff that's starting to try and link outcomes clearer to budgets? Yep. I'm unashamedly trying to leverage that great inquiry work, and to, I guess, not wait for the systemic changes which may or may not happen, but actually say, well...

I don't want to put words in the committee's mouth, but I think it was a pretty united conclusion in that report that we could do better, and that here are some examples of areas where we can do better. So we're using that to- I thought that was- Yeah... excellent, actually, to link government policy of the day- Yeah... to actually financials. Well done.

Question on 17 under infrastructure. You talked about infrastructure and obviously the challenges that we've had as a country. Good at spending money on it, not so good at bang for buck, and you identify that around the RCD piece. Yeah. You talked about maybe, well, you're going to track a large spend and track that through, but also you talked about incentives for public organizations to deliver better, and I just wondered if you could unpack that a bit. What would those incentives look like?

I don't want to attribute, but some of our programs have been very slow to get to spend, if we're honest. They're approved, but the delay, and as a nation, we draw debt down from the capital markets, and we incur interest costs holding that debt before the thing gets underway. And so should there be, and we don't have views on what the arrangements are, but in talking to Treasury, are there ways in which organizations that are causing the delay can effectively be exposed to some of those consequences of the

delay? There's a whole range of instruments. You could sheet the interest cost home to the project, for example, if you want to be blunt about it. But that's not for us to design, but we do want to understand, are the incentives not sufficiently creating the right tension for people to get on with it?

Is that similar to what I know some councils have used with, I'm trying to think the entities, where it's not a cost share, but there's an incentive on the agency. If they can save money through their spend, it's shared with the organization. Is that similar or- Yeah. Risk sharing or upside sharing arrangements are pretty standard features of commercial contracting situations.

So we just want, through our work, to explore whether or not those arrangements have a role to play in getting bang for buck through these- Yeah, sure... large projects. Megan. Sorry. Thank you. I think that debt spending track is a really interesting part, and the idea of sheeting those interest costs to the project.

In terms of, do you have any sense across a particular- Agency, have you done any looking at what that might actually look like in terms of shifting costs or saving costs? We haven't yet, but- Right... yeah. And, so a really good incentive. No agency's going to want to carry the increased interest costs on it.

Is there a kind of a parallel carrot that you could put in place there as well to incentivize better kind of faster moving on projects? Because obviously, there's going to have applications for the debt spending track there too. Yeah. There will be a range of positive incentives- Yeah... rather than whacking them with costs that can be- Yeah... built into it. And again, we're interested in how the processes that those spending entities are required to work themselves through.

Yeah. One of them could, and sorry, this is me just responding. This is not a position of the office. But there is lots of reflection on whether we've got the business case model right. Yeah. And the idea that some relief from some of the very detail heavy aspects, if you're an accredited organization with a track record of...

There are ways in which you can give relief through- Okay... stage gating. Sorry, I'm just trying to- No, that's really interesting. Thank you. I've got Todd and then Deborah. Oh, thanks. Thanks for being here. I'm just interested, actually, in the topic around Crown entity monitoring.

I know it looks, well, obviously you did some work a few years ago. Yeah. But keen just to get your thoughts on where you see that going, because I think this is really important because, yeah, obviously you've got some different departments, and I'm just thinking of like DIA, say, monitoring FENS, for example. Yeah. And some people might say that that hasn't been as effective as it could have been.

But I'm just keen to, yeah, get your initial thoughts. Have you identified particular monitoring entities you want to look at, or if that's still under development, and yeah, because this is pretty important because often they're probably maybe not doing it quite the- Yeah... job that ministers need. It's still in development, but if I look at some characteristics that I am very interested in, it's where we have a relatively small ministry or department monitoring a very large Crown entity.

I think that creates a particular type of power relationship which I wonder how the monitoring agency kind of works in that context. And I'm also interested, and these are formulative thoughts so hopefully the committee appreciate I'm just being open about- Yeah... our thinking.

Is there a way in which the monitoring function can move from being a passive recipient of ex-post reporting from the agency, putting that into a briefing note, and to a relationship they have with the entity they are monitoring, which is better understanding of context and strategic direction, and actually can have the tension in the relationship. But they're effectively like an equity analyst, so they are sufficiently senior and experienced that they can make a contribution back to the entity they are monitoring.

Not to get in the way of their independence, but I'm very keen to explore whether that model actually could work for the better aggregate performance of the ministry they're embedded in and the Crown entity. And I've road tested that with some of the central agencies, and we think there's ground to explore there. And I do know that the central agencies are actually working with some of the monitoring departments at the moment to think differently about the model, to think differently about the type of capability you put into your monitoring teams.

Yeah. Yeah. And there's no statutory barrier to them doing it in a different way. So I mean, what you're saying seems to make perfect sense to me, and it actually, I think, is what's needed because I think, yeah, as you said, at the moment, it's quite a passive relationship and we probably actually need to be a much more active monitor and identify issues earlier.

Would that be...? Yeah. And to be honest, when we're road testing these ideas, there's no resistance to the notion it could be improved, either by the departments who have monitoring responsibilities or the agencies they're monitoring. And hopefully we've got a contribution to make to the how.

And sorry, just one last quick last one. Obviously, from your previous experience, because obviously relatively new, you've been in the role-... not for a little while, but did you see, is that the kind of the way monitoring functions are moving in, say, even in the private sector or? Yeah. Well, if I look at the role, for example, a corporate treasury sitting at the heart of a multinational- Yeah... network in terms of its influence on capital allocation decisions made by autonomous subsidiaries.

I'm not saying that model is directly transferable, but it does- I mean-... seem to galvanize some focus on some strategic conversations as opposed to a passive kind of... Yeah. Very good. Thank you. Thank you. Dr. Deborah. Actually, that kind of follows on from this because as I was listening to how you're describing the work you're doing, it's within that monitoring space and how do we get- Agencies to do better and- Mm... so then who else does that work?

And of course, Treasury does it in various units within things. So it's quite a complex landscape of who's doing the monitoring- Mm... and the reporting back, and there's the reporting back to us obviously, and reporting back to the agencies. But then Treasury's got a much more internalized role in that as well. So it's a- Well, I do think this is a moment in time where machinery of government change is being contemplated.

Yeah. And so how you best design the system to monitor the delivery by those large Crown entities, yeah, I think it's a really timely question to be posed as we're looking at how agencies are pulled together potentially, and where responsibilities sit. And is the having monitoring activity happening in a range of places across the system, the right model?

Who knows? Yeah. I guess one of the things that's got me, just been thinking about it as we've been sitting here because you were talking about change and the way that after you go through change, structural change or whatever, you typically get a drop-off in performance, which is worth us being aware of because doesn't mean we shouldn't change stuff, it just means you've got to have a bit of an understanding of the context.

But I was thinking too, and this links back to some of the stuff we were worrying about with debt management track. If we do the monitoring wrong, we make public servants risk averse. And if we're too light touched, they take unnecessary risks. But if we're too heavy-handed, they won't take any risks at all. And I doubt there's even a sweet spot. There might be a range where it's kind of- Yeah... get the level of monitoring and reporting about right.

Have you been thinking that through? Yeah, and I think the most effective monitoring agencies have reached a meeting of minds with the entities they're monitoring around things they're going to be tight on. Yeah And things that they're going to be more permissive around or...

And I think the earlier in the relationship they can come to that meeting of minds, the better off and the better the monitoring works because the agency knows the things that are going to be under the microscope. And so almost if the only thing the monitoring entity does is reach that agreement, I think you'll see the downstream change in behaviors that would be in the interests of both parties.

Mm. Yes. But it's not a quick or easy process, so we can't... We've talked about this so much just in terms of the length of governments and things like that, and the pressure for us to deliver quick results. But we know that if we put that pressure on our state capacity, then we get mistakes.

But if we don't make some mistakes, then we don't make any... It's a complicated space. Yep. And the maturity of the accountability discussions kind of send pretty significant signals back into the public service about striking that balance, right? So if every mistake is met with the same reaction, you'll get changes in behavior, be they positive or negative, depending on the proportionality of the reaction to the situation.

Yeah. Just going to go to Dr. Dave Harrison. Yeah. I'm going to carry on with Todd and Deborah's line of thought here, because we're dealing with the Audit Office here, and when people think audit, they think financial. And yet we're moving to an outcomes-based performance measurement approach. And we're also talking about monitoring.

So we can monitor and see that the financials are fine. The problem is we may be actually doing the wrong things. The activities may not be correct, and we're not heading towards the outcomes we want to achieve. So I guess that's my question is, how do we actually think about it in terms of monitoring, to broaden that kind of thought process or get that inculcated into the monitoring agencies and so on?

Yeah, I think it's around saying that you are monitoring a relationship around results rather than controllables. And one of the themes which I've probably brushed over coming out of the work we've done this last 12 months is just the absence of evaluative work to enable agencies. We've pointed out that they don't report on impacts or results or outcomes. If you think, well, what enables them to do that, it is spending time and resource evaluating the effectiveness of the programs you run. And that

it's not for me to tell agencies where they should spend money, but it seems to be a critical inhibitor to the quality of performance reporting that we've all spent lots of time on. I'd have to look because there's something on here- No, there was just someone waving at me. Sorry. Oh, okay. One of my colleagues giving a to-er.

I'm with Ryan. We got a long way down that whole performance measurement and outcome work, which I think is fabulous. Yep. Now we're at the crunchy bit, aren't we, as to how do we actually make- Well, I understand some of my team are in front of the committee later in August- End of the month, yeah... to try and have a conversation about, well, irrespective, well, we will have the government response by then, but kind of irrespective of the response to the inquiry's final report, here are some things that we want your views on because they are the ways in which

we intend to work with committees to enhance scrutiny. And it's directly related to shifting our focus. And we've got to be careful. And I'm a chartered accountant, so it's not a move away from- No, exactly... financial integrity, right? It's an and.

Absolutely. Yeah. That's a good place to probably wrap up. But thank you very much, gentlemen. Thank you. Thank you. Andrew, your colleague, are you going to leave here with any burning regrets you didn't say anything? Just want to give you- No. They'll give me feedback on the way back to the office. Very good. Thanks for your time. Thank you. See you on the other side of the election.
Yeah. Good luck. Thank you. Thank you. 94 days to go. Not that you're counting, Des. 82 days to go to Advanced- Yes, that's right
